prompt: Rota should plan the return trip of a truck only once the yoghurt it carries has really left the Juiz de Fora plant. Which SAP record should Rota watch for?

choices.text: The status field on the sales order, which turns to shipped
choices.why: The order's status is a summary SAP computes for its own screens. The event is a document further down the chain.

choices.text: The outbound delivery created from the order
choices.why: The delivery is created when the warehouse is told to prepare the load. Nothing has left the plant yet.

choices.text: The goods issue
choices.why: Right: it is posted when the truck is loaded, it is the first step that changes the books, and it is the event itself rather than a summary of it.

choices.text: The incoming payment that clears the customer's open item
choices.why: The payment arrives about thirty days later. By then the truck has long come back.

prompt: A shop for consumers is added beside the Portal B2B, paid by Pix before anything ships. A developer proposes creating the billing document in SAP directly, since the money is already in. What breaks first?

choices.text: The NF-e, which the tax authority refuses for a payment made by Pix
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson ties the NF-e to how the customer pays. The damage is in the chain the invoice skips.

choices.text: Stock: no goods issue is posted, so the month-end count comes out short
choices.why: Right: the invoice points at no delivery, and the warehouse is never told. Entering the chain past the step the shop represents leaves every step before it unmade.

choices.text: Nothing breaks, because a paid invoice is exactly what the order would have produced in the end
choices.why: The end of the chain is reached, but the steps that move stock and tell the warehouse are never made, and the books stop agreeing with the cold store.

choices.text: The credit check, which blocks a customer without a credit limit
choices.why: A credit check runs on the sales order, which this shortcut never creates. It is skipped rather than triggered.

prompt: A goods issue for 80 cases was posted to Barbacena instead of Lavras. What does Serra Alta's SAP hold once the mistake is put right?

choices.text: One document, with the plant changed to Lavras
choices.why: A posted document is final. Editing it would let anybody change what the books said happened.

choices.text: One document for Lavras, after the wrong one was deleted
choices.why: Deleting the wrong one hides from the auditor that it ever existed, which is what the chain exists to prevent.

choices.text: Three documents: the wrong issue, its reversal and the right one
choices.why: Right: a mistake is corrected by a new document that reverses the old one, and an auditor sees all three.

choices.text: Two documents: the wrong issue, and a note on it pointing to Lavras
choices.why: A note does not move stock or cost. The books still say 80 cases left Barbacena.

prompt: Talita wants Salesforce to tell a supermarket buyer, during a visit, whether 2,000 cases of butter can be promised for Friday. A developer offers to copy SAP's stock table into Salesforce every night. Which objection is about the number itself, rather than about its age?

choices.text: The copy is up to a day old, so it misses what was sold this morning
choices.why: True, and it is about age. Even a copy made a second ago would carry the wrong figure.

choices.text: The table holds physical stock, not available-to-promise
choices.why: Right: available-to-promise subtracts reservations and quality blocks and adds stock in transit, and SAP's code does that sum. A copy of the table is current or stale, and wrong either way.

choices.text: Salesforce cannot store a table the size of SAP's stock
choices.why: Size is not what the lesson objects to. A small table copied perfectly would still hold the wrong figure.

choices.text: The copy would stop on Sunday nights, when SAP is down for maintenance
choices.why: A nightly copy taken before 01:00 survives the window. The calendar is a real constraint, and not the one about the meaning.

prompt: Joana's second design lets 4,000 bakeries see a figure SAP calculates. Why did she send a count of documents per month to the contracts team, before anybody wrote code?

choices.text: Because reading SAP's data through another system is still SAP use
choices.why: Right: SAP v Diageo upheld it in 2017. Indirect access is a licensing question before it is a technical one, and SAP now prices such use by the documents created.

choices.text: Because the count sizes the cache in front of the service
choices.why: The cache exists so that 4,000 bakeries do not become 4,000 calls, and it is sized by the engineers. The contracts team was asked something else.

choices.text: Because finance bills each bakery by the documents it creates
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson charges bakeries per document. The count is about what Serra Alta may owe SAP.

choices.text: Because a published service is licensed per call, unlike reading tables
choices.why: Reading the tables through a replica is still use of SAP's data in the contract. The door changed; the question did not go away.

prompt: Match each change at Serra Alta to the way of making SAP do it.

pairs.left: Choosing which taxes apply to a sale in Minas Gerais
A separate program that computes farm bonuses and calls SAP's published services
Adding code to SAP's own pricing program
Dropping a local way of numbering credit notes and using the one SAP ships

prompt: Which of these are master data at Serra Alta? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A farm, recorded in SAP as a supplier
choices.why: Right: it describes somebody Serra Alta deals with, changes slowly and is read by every module.

choices.text: Yesterday's goods receipt of that farm's milk
choices.why: A goods receipt records what happened. It is transactional, and it points at the farm rather than copying it.

choices.text: The material for whole UHT milk in one-litre cartons
choices.why: Right: one of about 2,600 active materials, created once and referred to by every order.

choices.text: A bakery's order for 40 cases of yoghurt
choices.why: An order is a transaction: it says customer and material by number and repeats neither.

prompt: The Rota team tests a release that posts goods receipts in SAP. A week later the trainers find dozens of strange receipts among the exercises their new users do. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: It connects to QAS client 300, the training client
choices.why: Right: an integration connects to a system and a client. With the wrong client it logs on, runs and posts into the training data without a single error.

choices.text: The test connection points at PRD, so the receipts reached production
choices.why: Then the receipts would be in client 100 of PRD, where the trainers do not work. Their data lives in QAS.

choices.text: A transport carried Rota's test data from DEV into QAS
choices.why: A transport carries programs and configuration. Business data stays in its client and does not travel that way.

choices.text: Programs are shared by every client, so the receipts show up in all of them
choices.why: Programs are shared, but business rows carry the client in their key. Orders in client 200 are invisible from 300.

prompt: A new interface calls BAPI_SALESORDER_CREATEFROMDAT2, gets an order number back and logs success. Nobody in VA03 can find the order. What did the interface leave out?

choices.text: Reading the returned message table, where the failure was reported
choices.why: That catches a different failure: an empty number read as success. Here a number came back.

choices.text: Waiting for the IDoc to reach status 53
choices.why: A BAPI over RFC is a synchronous call, not an IDoc. There is no status 53 to wait for.

choices.text: Calling BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT
choices.why: Right: a BAPI that writes does not commit on its own, and the caller got a number for an order that was never saved.

choices.text: Importing the call into PRD with a transport request
choices.why: Transports move programs and settings between systems. A call from outside is not transported.

prompt: Match each conversation with SAP to the door that suits it.

pairs.left: A supermarket chain's order arriving through the EDI provider
A bakery pressing confirm and waiting for an order number
A drivers' web app built by a team with no SAP libraries
The day's 1,900 collection lines from Coleta

right_distractors: An INSERT into the order tables

prompt: SAP's usage logging was switched on in January. In November a consultant proposes deleting every Z object that has not run since, to shrink the S/4HANA estimate. What does Edson object?

choices.text: Deleting is premature: the objects should be converted first and deleted after go-live
choices.why: Converting code nobody runs is the cost deletion saves. The lesson deletes first; the question is only when the evidence is enough.

choices.text: Ten months cannot see a program run only at the annual close
choices.why: Right: something used once a year looks dead to any measurement shorter than a year, which is why the reports were measured over a year and a quarter.

choices.text: Z objects are plug-ins outside the core, so they cost nothing in the conversion
choices.why: That was Joana's first reading, and Edson corrected it: a Z object lives inside SAP and each finding against the Simplification List has to be dealt with.

choices.text: Only SAP may delete a Z object, through its support
choices.why: Z and Y names are reserved for the customer precisely because the objects are the customer's own.

prompt: The board wants S/4HANA to open with fifteen years of history inside it and every customisation carried across, accepting that each item on SAP's list of changes must be dealt with first. Which approach is that?

choices.text: Greenfield, a new implementation
choices.why: Greenfield migrates master data, open items and balances, and leaves the history behind in the old system or an archive.

choices.text: Selective data transition, with the last three years
choices.why: That keeps what you choose, and the board chose everything. Picking three years is the opposite of the request.

choices.text: An upgrade from ECC 6.0, like the enhancement packages before it
choices.why: None of the three ways across is an upgrade. S/4HANA is the suite rewritten around a different data model.

choices.text: Brownfield, a system conversion
choices.why: Right: the existing system is converted in place and keeps history, customising and custom code, at the price of working through the Simplification List.

prompt: Serra Alta's order line table has 40 million lines, and its plant column holds one of three plants. Coded against a dictionary at two bits a line, as lesson 2 does it, how many megabytes does that column take?
A key-account rep leaves on Friday, and IT disables her Entra ID account that afternoon. On Monday, which of her ways in still works?

choices.text: None: every system at Serra Alta signs its users in through the tenant
choices.why: About half the estate trusts the tenant. SAP, Documentum and Coleta keep passwords of their own.

choices.text: Signing in to Salesforce with her password, through single sign-on
choices.why: Single sign-on is exactly what the disabled account blocks. The new sign-in fails.

choices.text: Her Salesforce API token, and her SAP password
choices.why: Right: single sign-on removes a password, not an account. The Salesforce user and its tokens stay, and SAP never asked the tenant.

choices.text: Her Teams chats, until the payroll provider closes her contract
choices.why: Teams signs in through Entra ID, so it is blocked at once. Nothing connects the payroll to the tenant in either direction.

prompt: A partner offers Felipe a faster way to post cheese invoices: change the posting routine in Business Central's base application. Why is that not on the table?

choices.text: Because AL is a language only Microsoft writes
choices.why: Partners write AL every day: Mantiqueira's six extensions are AL. What they cannot touch is the base.

choices.text: Because online, only extensions are allowed
choices.why: Right: nobody may modify the base, so the partner attaches an extension to the events Microsoft publishes. The product enforces lesson 1's middle ring, and that is why Felipe tests six extensions on update day instead of merging code.

choices.text: Because posting routines belong to Dataverse
choices.why: Business Central keeps its own database. Dataverse sits under the CRM apps and Power Apps.

choices.text: Because a change like that has to go through DEV, QAS and PRD first
choices.why: That is SAP's landscape. In Business Central online the base is closed to everybody, whatever the path.

prompt: A planner's flow reads the overdue receivables from SAP and saves a copy in his personal Gmail. Joana wants that stopped without breaking any of the 38 flows that read SAP. Which data loss prevention set-up does it?

choices.text: SAP in Blocked, so nothing copies receivables anywhere
choices.why: That is the policy Joana withdrew: 38 flows stop, among them one that updates credit limits nobody in IT knew about.

choices.text: SAP and Gmail both in Business, with the flow moved to a managed environment
choices.why: With both in one group the copy is allowed. A managed environment restricts who edits, not which connectors meet.

choices.text: Gmail in Blocked for the default environment only
choices.why: It works for the default environment and nowhere else; a flow rebuilt in another environment copies again. The lesson's policy splits groups across the tenant.

choices.text: SAP in Business and Gmail in Non-business
choices.why: Right: a flow may use one group or the other and never both, so the copy is refused and every flow that only reads SAP keeps running.

prompt: Match each flow to the tier Joana's proposal puts it in.

pairs.left: Saves the author's own email attachments to her OneDrive
Reads the day's milk intake and posts it in a plant's Teams channel
Updates customer credit limits in SAP from the committee's workbook

prompt: Whichever of the three options the group picks for its two ERPs, one piece of work removes the monthly re-keying of intercompany invoices. Which?

choices.text: Loading the NF-e XML that the seller already sends, authorised by SEFAZ, into the buyer's ERP
choices.why: Right: the data the clerk types already arrives structured and validated, and loading it needs neither ERP's API.

choices.text: Reading Business Central's trial balance through its API
choices.why: That serves the consolidation of option C. It moves balances once a month, not the invoices behind them.

choices.text: Linking the two document flows so a Serra Alta purchase order creates a Mantiqueira sales order
choices.why: That is option B itself, the one Joana argued against hardest, and it does nothing under A or C.

choices.text: Moving Business Central into Serra Alta's tenant
choices.why: That fixes who signs in where. The invoices would still be typed twice.

prompt: On the month-end night 34,000 invoices changed. Sent through sObject Collections, with each invoice naming its Account by the external id, how many API requests does the invoice sync make?

The Rota team wants a new flow that sends each day's truck arrivals to Salesforce, so reps can tell a store when its delivery comes. Its own load is small. What does Joana's rule ask of it before it goes live?

choices.text: Nothing, since a small flow cannot push the org over its allowance
choices.why: The month-end flow was small on an ordinary night too. The allowance is shared, and the sum of every flow's worst day is what crosses it.

choices.text: Its ordinary and worst-day request counts, summed with all others
choices.why: Right: the allowance is a budget the whole org shares, and the decision Joana recorded is that every integration declares its share of it.

choices.text: Enough parallel threads to finish before the reps start work
choices.why: That was Joana's first idea and it was wrong. The allowance counts requests, not time.

choices.text: A Bulk API 2.0 job, the tool every Salesforce integration now uses
choices.why: Joana's decision was explicitly not 'use the Bulk API'. A handful of daily arrivals has no need of a job.

prompt: A trigger on Visit__c queries the visit's Account once per record. It has run for years while reps save visits one by one. The first nightly load of visits, sent 200 per call, fails at once. Why?

choices.text: Bulk loads bypass triggers, so the Accounts are left without their visits
choices.why: If triggers were skipped there would be no failure to explain. The trigger ran, and ran 200 queries.

choices.text: The org ran out of its daily allowance of API requests
choices.why: 200 records in one call is one request. The failure is inside the transaction, not at the org's door.

choices.text: The 101st query in one 200-record transaction stops it all
choices.why: Right: a trigger receives up to 200 records per save, and code that queries inside the loop crosses the limit of 100 the moment records arrive in sets.

choices.text: The load ran slower than the 10 seconds of CPU time an Apex transaction gets
choices.why: CPU time is a real limit, and nothing here is slow. One query per record is what crosses a line.

prompt: Under Serra Alta's field table, which of these may be changed only in SAP? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A distributor's fiscal address
choices.why: Right: the NF-e depends on it, and the year both systems could edit it ended with a refused load.

choices.text: The category buyer at a supermarket chain
choices.why: Contacts belong to Salesforce and are not in SAP at all.

choices.text: A chain's credit limit
choices.why: Right: a rep asks for a change and never types one; the copy in Salesforce is read-only.

choices.text: The rep who looks after the account
choices.why: That is Salesforce's, and it is sent to SAP for the sales reports.

prompt: Edson's team adds a field to SAP's customer master to hold the Account's Salesforce Id. Why must it hold the 18-character form rather than the 15?

choices.text: Because the 15-character form expires when the Account is merged
choices.why: Merging is a separate matter. The two forms name the same record; they differ in how they survive comparison.

choices.text: Because SAP's search ignores case, and two 15s collide
choices.why: Right: the 15 is case-sensitive, and the three extra characters encode the capitals, so two Accounts never look like one.

choices.text: Because SAP customer numbers are ten characters and need room to grow
choices.why: That is the other id, in the other direction. The length of the SAP number is why SAP_Customer_Number__c is ten long.

choices.text: Because the CNPJ is fourteen digits and the id has to fit beside it
choices.why: The CNPJ finds duplicates; it is not the join, and the id does not sit beside it.

prompt: A Service Cloud case records which certificate of analysis an agent sent to a chain. Next year the certificate gets a corrected version. Which id should the case have stored?

choices.text: The version series id, so the case always opens the version in force
choices.why: That suits an instruction. The case is evidence of what was sent, and the series would open the correction instead.

choices.text: The id of the exact version sent
choices.why: Right: evidence points at what was true then, so the case keeps opening the certificate the chain received.

choices.text: The batch number, from which the certificate can be found again at any time
choices.why: A batch number alone can belong to two materials, and it finds the certificate's current version, not the one sent.

choices.text: The PDF's file name, which the lab can search for in Documentum
choices.why: Names are chosen by people and repeated by them; that is how the lab sent the wrong batch's certificate twice in 2025.

prompt: A link to a document version is evidence; a link to its version series is an instruction. Evidence points at what was true then, an instruction at what is true ___.

Serra Alta keeps a batch's certificate of analysis for five years, counted from the end of the year the batch was made, and disposes once a year in January. A batch is made on 2 December 2027. In which year does its certificate become eligible for disposal?
A consumer sues over a batch, and the legal department places a hold in Documentum on everything tied to it. The January disposal run skips those documents. What is still exposed?

choices.text: Nothing: the hold overrides every retention period, wherever it is kept
choices.why: It overrides every period in the system that obeys it. A hold the DMS obeys and the ERP's archive ignores is half a hold.

choices.text: The documents themselves, because IT may lift a hold at the next run
choices.why: A hold is placed and lifted by the people responsible for the case, not by IT.

choices.text: The batch's records kept in SAP and in Coleta
choices.why: Right: one batch has records in three systems, and a hold has to reach every one that holds part of the matter.

choices.text: The record of the disposal run itself
choices.why: That record is kept even when the records it lists are not. It is not what the run endangers.

prompt: Serra Alta moves its documents to another repository through CMIS. Which of these does CMIS carry across? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The files and their typed properties
choices.why: Right: objects and their metadata are the common ground every compliant repository exposes.

choices.text: Documentum's lifecycles and approval workflows
choices.why: Those are outside the common ground. The process that governs the documents has to be rebuilt in the new system.

choices.text: The versions of each document, as a version series
choices.why: Right: version series, check-out and check-in are part of the CMIS model.

choices.text: The retention schedule's rules
choices.why: Retention is Documentum's own, and it has to be configured again and tested before the first disposal run.

prompt: Serra Alta starts about 1,400 credit approvals a year, each lasting 4 days. If a new rule doubled that to 8 days, about how many credit approvals would be open at any moment, by Little's law?
In 2027 the three credit analysts are moved into a new shared-services group, and nobody opens the process designer. What does the credit approval process do next, and what would have caught it?

choices.text: It fails loudly on the first request, since the engine refuses a task for an empty group
choices.why: Nothing in the product complained about Fomento leiteiro for years. A task in an empty group is a quiet state unless somebody makes it an error.

choices.text: It reassigns the tasks to the CFO, who is the next approver
choices.why: The engine follows the model, and the model sends the analysis to the analysts' group. Nobody's list receives it.

choices.text: Requests wait unclaimed in an empty group; an age alert catches it
choices.why: Right: tasks go to groups so work survives people leaving, which makes the process depend on an organisation chart that changes without it.

choices.text: It keeps working, because the analysts take their task lists with them
choices.why: A task list is the group's, not the person's. That is what lets work survive a person leaving, and it is also the risk.

prompt: Match each need at Serra Alta to the family of tool the lesson's questions send it to.

pairs.left: Yearly supplier re-qualification: a buyer decides, an audit visit comes weeks later
Typing each new farm's 23 fields into Coleta's green screen
Emailing a customer the certificate when a batch is released, done in minutes
pairs.right: A low-code flow, with an owner

pairs.left: Turning each supermarket order into an EDI message

prompt: Denise merges two steps of supplier registration into one. Three of the open instances wait on one of the merged steps, and Vinícius chooses to migrate rather than drain. What must he decide for those three?

choices.text: Nothing: the engine keeps every instance on the version it started on
choices.why: That is what happens without a migration. He chose to migrate, so the instances move and need somewhere to stand.

choices.text: Whether to restart them from the first step of version 2
choices.why: Restarting throws away a month of a supplier's work, and it is not what migration tooling does. It moves or deletes tokens.

choices.text: Where each token now stands: moved to another step, or deleted
choices.why: Right: a token on a step that no longer exists is orphaned, and somebody has to decide its place step by step.

choices.text: Which of the two old steps' forms the merged step should open
choices.why: The forms are part of designing version 2, for the instances to come. The question about the three in flight is where they stand.

prompt: 315 supplier registrations failed at the call that creates the vendor in SAP, nearly all of them on Sunday between 01:00 and 05:00. Which fix answers the cause?

choices.text: Tell buyers not to finish a registration on Saturday nights
choices.why: That moves the burden onto people and fails the first time somebody forgets. The step itself has to know the window.

choices.text: A retry that knows SAP's window, and an owner for failures
choices.why: Right: the step failed because SAP was down on purpose, and a failed instance that nobody looks at is how SAP and the engine came to disagree.

choices.text: Let buyers create the vendor in SAP by hand whenever it is missing
choices.why: That is what happened, and it left 315 histories saying 'not registered' about suppliers SAP has.

choices.text: Rebuild the process on the integration bus
choices.why: The bus would meet the same Sunday window. Moving the step does not give it a calendar.

prompt: In a draft of supplier registration, a parallel gateway starts three checks at once, and an exclusive gateway joins them before 'Create vendor in SAP'. Walked with the token game, what happens?

choices.text: The vendor is created once, after all three checks finish
choices.why: That is what a parallel join would do. An exclusive join does not wait; it lets every arriving token through.

choices.text: The instance waits for ever at the join
choices.why: That is the opposite mistake, an exclusive split closed by a parallel join. Here three tokens exist and all of them pass.

choices.text: The vendor is created three times
choices.why: Right: the parallel split made three tokens, the exclusive join passes each one through, and the step after it runs once per token.

choices.text: The engine refuses to deploy a model whose split and join differ
choices.why: The notation does not require matching blocks, and no engine is said to refuse one. The model runs, which is the danger.

prompt: A farm phones after three weeks. Its instance shows as running, and nobody's task list holds anything for it. Which modelling mistake fits best?

choices.text: An exclusive split closed by a parallel join
choices.why: Right: the split sent one token, the join counts two incoming flows and waits for a token that was never created. A deadlock looks exactly like a slow instance.

choices.text: A parallel split closed by an exclusive join
choices.why: That runs the next step twice, which would put a duplicate task in somebody's list rather than an empty one.

choices.text: A gateway labelled as a task, such as 'Check quality'
choices.why: A badly labelled gateway is a modelling smell; it would still route the token somewhere.

choices.text: Two sequence flows drawn straight into one task
choices.why: Uncontrolled flow starts the task again per token; it duplicates work rather than stalling it.

prompt: In credit approval, a limit above R$ 150,000 needs the CFO, and a customer with overdue invoices needs a review by collections. A request can need one, both or neither. Which split fits after the analysis?

choices.text: An exclusive gateway, with one condition per reviewer
choices.why: An exclusive split sends exactly one token, so a request needing both reviews would get only one of them.

choices.text: A parallel gateway, so both reviews always run
choices.why: A parallel split takes no conditions; every request would go to the CFO and to collections.

choices.text: An event-based gateway on the two approvals
choices.why: An event-based gateway picks whichever event happens first. Here the choice is by data known before the split.

choices.text: An inclusive gateway, with a default flow, closed by an inclusive join
choices.why: Right: each true condition gets a token, the default covers 'no extra review', and the matching join waits for exactly the tokens that were sent.

prompt: Joana draws credit approval as a collaboration diagram. Which of these should be pools rather than lanes? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The credit bureau that returns a score
choices.why: Right: it runs its own process and decides for itself, so Serra Alta sends a request and waits for an answer.

choices.text: The three credit analysts in finance
choices.why: One process directs their work through a task list. They are a lane.

choices.text: The distributor asking for terms
choices.why: Right: Serra Alta cannot assign it work, only exchange messages with it.

choices.text: Marcos Teles, who approves large limits
choices.why: He receives a task in Serra Alta's own process. A role inside the process is a lane.

prompt: In the model, the 10-day timer on the quality visit is written P10D. The 30-day wait for a signed contract, as an ISO 8601 duration, is ___.
Two things can go wrong at 'Create farm in SAP': SAP refuses because the farmer's CPF already belongs to another vendor, or SAP does not answer at all. Which belongs in the model as a BPMN error?

choices.text: Both, each with its own error boundary event
choices.why: Modelling every timeout as an error fills the diagram with paths the business does not recognise and hides the ones it does.

choices.text: The refusal: the business has a response to it
choices.why: Right: an existing vendor is an outcome somebody acts on. A silent SAP is retried by the engine and becomes an incident when the retries run out.

choices.text: The silence, because it stops the process
choices.why: There is nothing to tell the farm about a timeout. The response is to try again, which is the engine's job, not a path in the diagram.

choices.text: Neither: errors belong in the code that calls SAP
choices.why: A business outcome with a known response is exactly what a BPMN error event is for.

prompt: A farm is turned down at the document check, before the parallel split that registers its bank account. The path ends in a compensation end event. What does the compensation do?

choices.text: It runs 'Cancel registration' as usual
choices.why: Compensation runs only for activities that completed. This account was never registered.

choices.text: It rolls the bank's database back to before the application arrived
choices.why: No transaction stays open across a bank and thirty days. Compensation is a new action, not a rollback.

choices.text: Nothing, because nothing in its scope completed that needs undoing
choices.why: Right: an activity that never finished has nothing to compensate, so the end event triggers no handler.

choices.text: It throws an error for the field team to handle
choices.why: Compensation and error are different events. The refusal is a normal outcome and needs no error.

prompt: Joana and Denise want to answer 'where is farm 4471?' at any moment. Why does that push onboarding towards orchestration rather than choreography?

choices.text: Because choreography cannot carry messages between pools
choices.why: Choreography is built from messages. What it lacks is a single participant who knows the whole sequence.

choices.text: Because an orchestrator holds the state of every instance in one place
choices.why: Right: in choreography nobody can answer without asking every participant; the price is that each one depends on the conductor.

choices.text: Because BPMN 2.0 has no choreography diagrams
choices.why: It has them; few tools execute them.

choices.text: Because the farm and the bank would have to become lanes
choices.why: In the orchestration they stay pools, exchanging messages. Only Serra Alta's own process is inside.

prompt: Serra Alta's bus connects twelve systems today. If two more were added, how many point-to-point connections would be possible between the fourteen?
Rota's adapter gets HTTP 500 from FarmRegistry. Inside is a soap:Client fault whose detail is FarmNotFound. What should the adapter do?

choices.text: Return 'unknown farm' and never retry
choices.why: Right: Client means the request itself is the problem, so sending it again gets the same answer. The 500 is how SOAP 1.1 sends every fault.

choices.text: Retry once after two seconds, then fall back to yesterday's tank
choices.why: That is the answer to soap:Server, when the service failed and the request may have been fine.

choices.text: Treat it as the bus being down, since status 500 means the server failed
choices.why: In SOAP 1.1 the status is 500 for every fault, so the status says nothing about whose fault it is. The faultcode does.

choices.text: Raise an error and alert the Rota team about a bug in its request
choices.why: That fits a Client fault with no known detail. A declared FarmNotFound is an answer with a meaning: the farm left or the code is wrong.

prompt: After a patch, a partner's SOAP service starts answering with env: in front of every element where it used to write soap:. The namespace URIs are the same. What changed in the message?

choices.text: The SOAP version, from 1.1 to 1.2
choices.why: The version is told by the envelope's namespace, and that did not change.

choices.text: The contract, so the client should be generated again
choices.why: A new contract would carry a new namespace. Prefixes are not part of it.

choices.text: The security header, which now needs mustUnderstand
choices.why: Nothing about the header is in the change. Only a local name for the same namespace moved.

choices.text: Nothing in its meaning
choices.why: Right: a prefix is a local name for a namespace. A real XML parser does not notice; text matching on soap: breaks, as Rota's regular expressions did.

prompt: SOAP 1.1 names its two main fault codes Client and Server. SOAP 1.2, used by the NF-e web services, names them Sender and ___.
By lesson 8's test, which of these flows carry business logic? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: One that rewrites 20261022 as 2026-10-22
choices.why: Changing a format is integration. Nobody outside IT would ask for it to change.

choices.text: One that holds back orders from customers with an overdue invoice
choices.why: Right: that is a credit policy, however short the code, and finance could ask for it to change.

choices.text: One that takes orders off an MQ queue and posts them over HTTP
choices.why: Bridging a protocol is what a dumb pipe does. It decides nothing about the business.

choices.text: One that picks Lavras or Juiz de Fora by the latitude of the chain's warehouse
choices.why: Right: which plant ships is a logistics decision, and a planner would recognise it and argue with it.

prompt: Put the work of shrinking Serra Alta's bus in the order lesson 8 gives it.
items: Freeze new business logic in flows
List every flow, with a year of traffic
Switch off the dead flows, through a month-end
Move transformations out as their owners touch them
Move orchestrations out, one decision at a time
trap: Without the freeze, every week of inventory adds flows to move; and the dead go before anything moves because switching them off shrinks every step after it.

prompt: Lewis and Fowler's 'dumb pipe' is easy to misread. Which of these would a dumb pipe still do at Serra Alta?

choices.text: Give bakeries 3% off orders above R$ 1,800
choices.why: A discount is a business decision. That is exactly what the pipe stops doing; it belongs in SAP's pricing.

choices.text: Block an order whose customer is over the limit
choices.why: That is a credit policy, and SAP's own credit management already does it with the right limit.

choices.text: Hold an order in MQ until SAP is back from its Sunday window
choices.why: Right: dumb is not unreliable. Holding, retrying and delivering to a declared destination all leave the business alone.

choices.text: Choose which plant ships each line of an EDI order
choices.why: Which plant ships is the logistics planners' decision, put in the bus only because it saw the order first.

prompt: Someone argues that the 14 services Salesforce calls are protected at message level, because each request carries a UsernameToken in its SOAP header. What is wrong with the argument?

choices.text: A UsernameToken is not valid in SOAP 1.1
choices.why: FarmRegistry is SOAP 1.1 and demands one. The token is legal; it is the protection that is misjudged.

choices.text: It is as safe as the TLS around it, no safer
choices.why: Right: the password travels as PasswordText. It is message-level in form and connection-level in protection. Nothing is signed or encrypted, and the bus reads it in clear.

choices.text: mustUnderstand makes the receiver ignore the token
choices.why: It does the opposite: a receiver that does not know the block must refuse the message.

choices.text: Message-level protection only exists in WS-AtomicTransaction
choices.why: Message-level protection is WS-Security's: XML Signature and XML Encryption. None of the 70 flows uses either.

prompt: The stock check runs portal → ESB → SAP, each about 99.5% available. If a fourth hop at 99.5% were added to the chain, what would its availability be, in percent, to one decimal place?
Coleta's loader adds up the farm lines and compares them with the trailer before posting anything. Which of these failures does that check let straight through?

choices.text: A file cut off after 1,200 of its 1,900 lines
choices.why: The cut file has no trailer, or a short last line, and the shape check refuses it before any total is read.

choices.text: A farm line deleted by hand to fix another line
choices.why: The trailer still promises the old count and litres, so the sums disagree and the file is refused.

choices.text: A whole, correct file loaded a second time
choices.why: Right: a repeat is internally perfect. Only a loader that remembers the day and sequence it has loaded can refuse it, as the 2019 double count showed.

choices.text: A farm's litres changed from 960 to 690 in transit
choices.why: The farm lines then add up to 270 litres fewer than the trailer says, and the check catches it.

prompt: A new chain goes Rota → ESB → Coleta. Rota waits 5 seconds for the ESB; the ESB waits 30 seconds for Coleta and retries twice. On a slow night, what goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, since the ESB has more patience than Rota needs
choices.why: The ESB's patience is the problem: it keeps Coleta working for 25 seconds after the only caller stopped listening.

choices.text: Wasted work, multiplied by repeats
choices.why: Right: the ESB keeps Coleta busy for answers nobody waits for. The deeper the hop, the shorter the timeout, and retrying into a struggling system adds load, as the stock check's closing week showed.

choices.text: Rota fails first, but its error tells the ESB to stop
choices.why: A caller that gives up sends nothing down the chain. The ESB goes on waiting on its own clock.

choices.text: The ESB answers too fast and Rota reads a partial reply
choices.why: Nothing here is fast. The trouble is waits set separately, each sensible alone and wrong together.

prompt: Which of these messages is a command rather than an event?

choices.text: Farm 017605 was suspended
choices.why: A fact in the past tense, for any number of receivers to act on as they choose.

choices.text: Barbacena's intake plan changed
choices.why: This is how lesson 9 publishes the plant intake: a fact Rota and anybody else may subscribe to.

choices.text: Invoice 4711 was authorised
choices.why: The model event of the lesson: the publisher does not know who listens and expects nothing back.

choices.text: Create farm 017605 as a vendor in SAP
choices.why: Right: an imperative for one receiver chosen by the sender, who expects it done. A queue removes the coupling in time and keeps the coupling in knowledge.

prompt: When the lab rejects a farm's milk, Rota must skip the farm tomorrow, Coleta must mark the collection, and farm relations must phone the farmer. Nobody is waiting at a screen. Which style fits, by lesson 9's table?

choices.text: A call from the lab system to each of the three
choices.why: Nobody is waiting, and the lab would have to know and reach all three, failing part-way when one is down, like the old invoice flow.

choices.text: An event, published once
choices.why: Right: one fact, several consumers, nobody waiting. Each subscribes and decides what to do, and a fourth needs no change at the lab.

choices.text: A nightly file to each consumer
choices.why: A file is as old as its last run; Rota would plan the morning's trucks before learning the farm was rejected.

choices.text: A shared table the three poll
choices.why: That is a queue built from a table, with nobody watching its error rows and a poll's delay on every reader.

prompt: The portal's invoice consumer stops during a deployment and never restarts. It logs nothing. Which alarm finds this?

choices.text: An alarm on errors from the consumer
choices.why: A stopped consumer produces no errors at all. That is why this failure hides.

choices.text: An alarm when SAP's invoice publication fails
choices.why: SAP publishes normally; the publisher does not wait for any consumer and cannot see one stop.

choices.text: An alarm on the age of the oldest message nobody has consumed
choices.why: Right: an event integration fails as a lag, not an error, so the alarm watches the lag.

choices.text: An alarm on the count of invoices issued per day
choices.why: SAP still issues about 1,400 a day; the count is normal while the portal falls days behind.

prompt: The ABAP job reads pedido_integracao, creates a sales order in SAP and then sets the row to P. It crashes between the two steps. What happens on its next run?

choices.text: The order is created in SAP a second time
choices.why: Right: the row still says N, so the job sees new work. It is the double load of the file section in another form.

choices.text: The row is moved to E, with SAP's message
choices.why: E is set when SAP refuses an order. Here SAP accepted it and nobody recorded that.

choices.text: SAP refuses the order as a duplicate
choices.why: Nothing in the design lets SAP recognise the second order as the first. Lesson 10 is about giving it that.

choices.text: The portal resends the order
choices.why: The portal wrote the row once and waits. The repeat comes from the job reading the same row.

prompt: Rota stops reading Coleta's farm table and takes change data capture events from Coleta's journal instead. Sebastião then splits the address field in two. What does Rota see?

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the journal hides the table's columns
choices.why: A CDC event is a row, before and after. The journal carries the table's shape, not a contract of its own.

choices.text: Rows whose shape follows the new table
choices.why: Right: CDC removes the load and the polling but moves the coupling rather than removing it. A translator into business events is what absorbs the change.

choices.text: A gap: CDC misses changes to the schema
choices.why: Every committed change comes out of the log in order. What arrives is complete, and shaped like the new table.

choices.text: An error from Coleta, which refuses the split while a reader is attached
choices.why: The owner does not know the reader is there. Nothing stops him changing his own table.

prompt: A consumer retries with exponential backoff, waiting 1 second, then 2, then 4, and so on. With six retries instead of the lesson's five, how many seconds does it spend waiting in all?

To be safe, a colleague changes consumer.py to commit the message id in its own transaction first, then apply the payment in a second one. The process dies between the two. What happens when the broker redelivers?

choices.text: The payment is applied twice
choices.why: That is the other wrong arrangement, recording the id after the work. Here the id is already there.

choices.text: The broker sends it to the dead-letter queue
choices.why: Nothing failed on the redelivery; the consumer acknowledged a message it believes it handled.

choices.text: The payment is applied once, correctly
choices.why: It would be, if both rows committed together. Split in two, one can be true without the other.

choices.text: The redelivery is skipped and the payment is lost
choices.why: Right: the id says done and the work never happened. It is at-most-once by a longer road; only one transaction for both closes the gap.

prompt: A consumer first runs SELECT on the processed table and inserts the id only if nothing is found. It passes every test. Under which condition does it apply a payment twice?

choices.text: When two instances check before either commits
choices.why: Right: the check and the insert are two steps, and another consumer acts between them. A primary key decides for both.

choices.text: When the same message is redelivered a day later
choices.why: By then the first copy committed its id, so the SELECT finds it. The danger is two copies at once.

choices.text: When the message has no natural key
choices.why: The check works on the message id, which every message carries. The race is about timing, not about keys.

choices.text: When the broker runs at-most-once
choices.why: At-most-once loses messages rather than repeating them.

prompt: A new consumer stores payments with a unique constraint on the invoice number, so a repeated payment message is ignored. A bakery pays NF-18232 in two instalments. What happens?

choices.text: Both instalments are recorded, since they arrive as two messages
choices.why: The constraint is on the invoice, not on the message. Two messages about one invoice collide.

choices.text: The second instalment is dropped as if it were a duplicate
choices.why: Right: a natural key is right only where the business says the fact happens once. A payment is not unique per invoice, which is why consumer.py uses the message id.

choices.text: The second instalment waits in a resequencer
choices.why: Nothing here is out of order. The constraint refuses it outright.

choices.text: The broker redelivers the second until the first is cleared
choices.why: The broker knows nothing of the constraint; the consumer acknowledges what it skipped.

prompt: Put the life of one portal payment, from the outbox to the consumer's ledger, in order.
items: The payment row and its outbox row commit in one transaction
The relay reads the unsent rows in id order
The relay publishes the message
The relay marks the row sent
The consumer records the id and applies the payment together
trap: Publishing before marking is what makes a crash produce a duplicate rather than a loss, and the consumer's single transaction is what makes the duplicate harmless.

prompt: A developer changes the relay to stamp each message with a fresh id at the moment it publishes. The relay crashes after publishing and before marking the row sent, then restarts. What does the consumer do?

choices.text: It applies the payment twice
choices.why: Right: the same payment arrives under two ids, and the processed table sees two different messages. The id has to be fixed when the outbox row is written.

choices.text: It skips the copy, as it did with portal-1
choices.why: portal-1 was skipped because both copies carried the id fixed in the outbox row. With fresh ids there is nothing to match.

choices.text: It never sees the payment
choices.why: The row was still unsent, so the restarted relay publishes it again. Nothing is lost.

choices.text: It refuses both, as a conflict
choices.why: Two different ids are two different messages to the consumer; there is nothing for it to see as a conflict.

prompt: Which of these failures should send a message straight to its dead-letter queue, without spending retries? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The JSON in the message does not parse
choices.why: Right: the problem is in the message, and the hundredth try fails like the first.

choices.text: SAP is in its Sunday maintenance window
choices.why: Transient: the same message succeeds unchanged after 05:00.

choices.text: The order names a customer that does not exist in SAP
choices.why: Right: no amount of waiting creates the customer. It is permanent.

choices.text: Salesforce refuses the call because a limit was reached
choices.why: Transient: when the window rolls forward, the same call goes through.

prompt: SAP sends each customer's credit status to Salesforce as a value with SAP's change number. A replay from the dead-letter queue delivers 'open, version 12' after 'blocked, version 15' was applied. With a conditional update on the version, what happens?

choices.text: The customer reopens, since the replay is the newest delivery
choices.why: Delivery order is not version order. Without the check, this is the butter price reversal again.

choices.text: The consumer holds it until versions 13 and 14 arrive
choices.why: Holding is for messages that state a change. A stated value that is older carries nothing the consumer needs.

choices.text: No row changes, and the message is acknowledged
choices.why: Right: version 15 already contains everything that matters, so the old value is discarded with no read and no race.

choices.text: It goes back to the dead-letter queue
choices.why: Nothing failed: an old value that changes nothing is a normal outcome, acknowledged and done.

prompt: A distributor's weekly order is split into three messages, one per plant, and an aggregator completes when three replies arrive. One branch's credentials expire and its message goes to a dead letter queue. What does the distributor receive?

choices.text: A confirmation of the two plants that answered
choices.why: That is what a count with a timeout sends. With only a count, the aggregator never decides the set is finished.

choices.text: An error message from the aggregator
choices.why: Nothing has failed from the aggregator's point of view. It is still waiting, and waiting raises nothing.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right: an aggregator with only a count waits for ever for a reply that will never come, as nine of Vale Verde's orders did in March.

choices.text: Two confirmations, one for the original and one when the branch is fixed
choices.why: That is the late-reply problem, and it needs a timeout to have fired first. Here nothing has closed yet.

prompt: An aggregator now completes at 21 replies or after 30 minutes. Business Central answers the cheese message ten minutes after the timeout fired. If the aggregator has forgotten the order, what happens?

choices.text: The late reply is dropped, since its order was confirmed
choices.why: Dropping it needs the aggregator to know the order was closed, which it has forgotten.

choices.text: A second, nearly empty confirmation, much later
choices.why: Right: the reply opens a new aggregate, waits for 20 siblings that never come and times out. An aggregator has to remember which aggregates it closed, for longer than its timeout, so a late arrival raises a correction instead.

choices.text: It is added to the confirmation already sent
choices.why: A sent confirmation cannot be edited; something has to recognise the reply and send a correction.

choices.text: The router sends it to the invalid message channel
choices.why: The router sits before the ERPs; a reply never passes through it.

prompt: Match each routing pattern to what goes in and what comes out.

pairs.right: One message in; the same message out, on one of several channels
One message in; the same message out, or nothing
One message in; several smaller messages out
Several messages in; one message out

right_distractors: One message in; the same message out with data added

prompt: With every system talking to every other, point to point needs n(n − 1) translators and a canonical model needs 2n. Counting systems one by one, a canonical model first saves translators at the ___ system.

Rota's team draws a new asynchronous flow that adds each farm's tank size, looked up in Coleta, to every GPS reading a truck sends. What does the content enricher bring into the flow that the drawing hides?

choices.text: A synchronous call per message, so the flow inherits Coleta's availability
choices.why: Right: on the diagram it is one more icon; underneath, every reading waits on Coleta, and a flow handling a reading from every truck cannot afford that call. A cache or replicated reference data defuses it.

choices.text: A second copy of every reading, sent to a message store
choices.why: That is a wire tap. An enricher adds data to the message on its way; it sends no copies.

choices.text: A larger message, which IBM MQ refuses over 4 MB
choices.why: A tank size adds a few bytes. The 4 MB limit is the claim check's concern, with PDFs.

choices.text: Nothing, because enrichment happens inside the bus
choices.why: Where the step runs does not change what it calls. The lookup still reaches Coleta.

prompt: Lavras opens a new line under a new plant code, and nobody tells the integration team. In Joana's first design, with one order queue read by selective consumers, what happens to that line's orders?

choices.text: SAP's consumer takes them, since it selects everything that is not Alagoa
choices.why: In that design the SAP side selected its own plants. A code nobody listed matches no selector.

choices.text: They go to the invalid message channel
choices.why: That is the content-based router's default exit, the design Rui argued for. Selectors have no default.

choices.text: The queue manager returns them to the portal
choices.why: Nothing is returned; the message was delivered to the queue successfully.

choices.text: They sit on the queue for ever, and nobody is told
choices.why: Right: a message no selector matches waits on a queue that looks healthy. A router gives the decision one place and a default exit.

prompt: The SAP branch reads a store order under syncpoint and calls the BAPI. SAP commits the sales order, then the flow fails before committing its get. What stops a second sales order?

choices.text: The unit of work, which rolls back the sales order
choices.why: SAP's commit is not part of MQ's unit of work. The transaction protects the message, not the order.

choices.text: A check that SAP has no order yet for that chain order, store and plant
choices.why: Right: the message goes back on the queue and is read again, so the receiver has to be idempotent as well as transactional.

choices.text: The aggregator, which ignores the second reply
choices.why: By then SAP has already created two orders; the aggregator only collects what they say.

choices.text: Nothing: a message read under syncpoint is never read twice
choices.why: Syncpoint is what puts the message back on the queue after the failure. It is read twice on purpose.

prompt: Which change would have let finance find the Barbacena farm's rejected payment within minutes, by lesson 11?

choices.text: A table mapping each hop's identifier to the next
choices.why: That is the arrangement the rule replaces. Each hop inventing a name keeps the trail cold.

choices.text: A channel purger on the remittance queue
choices.why: Purging deletes payments; it finds nothing.

choices.text: SAP's payment number in the CNAB field the bank returns
choices.why: Right: pick the identifier at the first hop where it exists and carry it unchanged, so a rejected line points at a document and the document at a vendor.

choices.text: A test message through the flow every morning at 05:00
choices.why: A test message proves the flow works; it does not name a real payment.

prompt: SAP is unavailable for 3 hours on a weekday evening while bakeries keep ordering at about 120 orders an hour, all accepted for later confirmation. The job that creates them in SAP handles about 360 an hour. How many hours does the backlog take to clear once SAP is back?
Rui proposes a second bus node, quoting 1 − 0.005² = 99.9975%. Joana goes through last year's outage record with him first. Why does the pair come out nearer 99.79%?

choices.text: Because two nodes double the chance that one of them fails
choices.why: One failing is harmless when the other carries the work. The loss comes from failures both nodes share.

choices.text: Because the formula needs three nodes to hold
choices.why: The formula is for two copies. What it needs is independence, which real failures break.

choices.text: Because some failures hit both nodes at once
choices.why: Right: an expired certificate and a bad deployment take both nodes down together. 18 of the 43.8 hours had shared causes that stay whatever the number of nodes. Redundancy removes only the independent failures.

choices.text: Because SAP's 99.0% caps the pair
choices.why: SAP caps the chain, not the bus pair. The pair's own figure falls short for a reason inside the bus.

prompt: Rui's team promises the portal team that the bus will answer 99.9% of calls over 30 days. If it does not, there is no credit, only a review with both teams. By lesson 12's test, what is it?

choices.text: An objective, with an internal promise's consequences
choices.why: Right: what happens if it is missed is a review, a budget and a freeze, nothing anybody collects. Calling it an SLA only makes it sound enforceable.

choices.text: An SLA, since it is a number two teams agreed in writing
choices.why: Agreement in writing is not the test. The test is a consequence somebody can collect, and there is none.

choices.text: An indicator, since it is measured over a window
choices.why: The indicator is the measurement, the share of calls answered. The 99.9% target over 30 days is something else.

choices.text: An error budget
choices.why: The budget is what the objective leaves over, 0.1% of calls. It follows from the promise; it is not the promise.

prompt: Which of these changes would break the contract of Coleta's nightly file to SAP? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A new field added at the end of every line
choices.why: Right: SAP's loader checks the length of each line, and a fixed-width reader cannot tell an extra field from a shifted one.

choices.text: The file arriving at 04:00 on a weekday instead of by 01:30
choices.why: Right: timing is part of the contract, and a load that runs at 02:00 finds nothing.

choices.text: A second consumer starting to read the same file
choices.why: Nothing the producer sends changes, and SAP's load keeps working. That is a new entry in the registry, not a break.

choices.text: The date field carrying the day of loading instead of the day of collection
choices.why: Right: every line still parses, and Saturday's milk is paid as Sunday's. A change of meaning is the break that passes every check.

prompt: Supermarket orders cross the EDI provider, the bus and SAP. SAP stops on Sundays 01:00–05:00 and the bus 01:00–03:00. If the EDI provider set its maintenance for Sundays 04:00–06:00, how much planned downtime would the chain have each week?

choices.text: 4 hours, SAP's window, since the others overlap it
choices.why: The bus's window sits inside SAP's; the provider's last hour does not.

choices.text: 8 hours, the sum of the three windows
choices.why: Windows that overlap are not counted twice. The chain is down for their union.

choices.text: 2 hours, the provider's own window
choices.why: The chain needs every member up, so every member's window counts.

choices.text: 5 hours, from 01:00 to 06:00
choices.why: Right: the planned downtime of a chain is the union of its members' windows. Moving the provider inside SAP's window would bring it back to four.

prompt: The Portal B2B backs up its uploaded files at 01:00 and its database at 03:00. A test restore finishes cleanly. What should Joana expect to find?

choices.text: Nothing wrong, since each backup reported success
choices.why: Each succeeded, as Documentum's did for sixteen years. Success of the parts says nothing about their agreement.

choices.text: Files from between 01:00 and 03:00 with no record pointing at them
choices.why: That is the mirror image the order would produce if the database came first. Here the database is the later of the two.

choices.text: Records of uploads made between 01:00 and 03:00 whose files are missing
choices.why: Right: two backups of one system taken at different moments restore to a state that never existed, as the 37 certificates showed.

choices.text: A restore that took longer than the RTO
choices.why: Nothing here is about duration; the restore finished. The defect is in what it restored.

prompt: Coleta's own backup is a nightly save, yet its collections have an effective RPO of zero, because every handheld keeps seven days. An RPO belongs to the ___, not only to the machine that stores it.
Put the steps of a degraded-mode runbook in the order lesson 12 gives them.
items: Detect, by an alarm on an objective
Declare the mode, by a named person, with the time
Switch the fallback on
Tell the people affected
Drain what accumulated
Reconcile, and close the mode
trap: Draining comes after the dependency is back and takes time of its own; reconciling last checks that everything done in the mode arrived exactly once.

prompt: A consultancy proposes replacing Coleta in three stages: first all its data into PostgreSQL, then its logic into services, then its screens. Why does lesson 13 reject the plan?

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL cannot read IBM i journals
choices.why: The database is not the objection. Any target would have the same problem when the layers move one at a time.

choices.text: Because it is a big bang in a strangler's clothes
choices.why: Right: nothing a caller asks for moves until the last layer does, because every capability needs all three layers, so the risk is retired at the end, all at once. A slice cuts through every layer for one capability.

choices.text: Because the screens have to move first, so the clerks are trained early
choices.why: Moving screens first is still slicing by layer. The order of the layers is not the fault.

choices.text: Because Coleta's data cannot leave the IBM i before Sebastião retires
choices.why: Data leaves Coleta from phase 1, through change data capture. The timing of his retirement shapes the end date, not the slicing.

prompt: Once farm lookup is routed through the facade, the Rota team asks for one small favour: have the facade convert Coleta's volumes into litres before replying. What does lesson 13 say?

choices.text: Yes, because the facade sees every request and is the cheapest place
choices.why: That is the temptation the rule names. Each such favour makes the facade a third system that has to be migrated too.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the route can still be turned back
choices.why: Reversibility is a separate rule. A route that computes is still a facade with logic of its own.

choices.text: No: the facade routes and does not compute; the translation belongs to the new side
choices.why: Right: the facade decides where a request goes and nothing about the answer. Translating Coleta's words is the anti-corruption layer's job.

choices.text: No, because Coleta must be changed to send litres
choices.why: Changing Coleta is exactly what the migration keeps to a minimum.

prompt: Six clerks correct collections on green-screen terminals, and the change exists only once Coleta writes it to its tables. Which technique gets those corrections to the new collection service?

choices.text: Capturing what the journals record
choices.why: Right: the only place to pick the change up is afterwards, in the database's own record of changes. It gives rows, not intentions, so the layer interprets them.

choices.text: Event interception at the docking PC
choices.why: That catches the handheld files on their way in. A clerk's correction never passes there.

choices.text: Branch by abstraction inside Coleta
choices.why: Branch by abstraction is for code you own and change freely. Changing Coleta is what the plan avoids.

choices.text: A dual write from the terminal to both systems
choices.why: The terminal is Coleta's own; nothing can be added to it, and a dual write is the shortcut the plan forbids.

prompt: A journal row arrives saying farm 041327's status changed to a letter the team has never seen. What should the anti-corruption layer do?

choices.text: Map it to 'suspended for quality', the safest status for a farm
choices.why: Guessing puts a wrong fact into the new system in a clean format, which is worse than a visible error.

choices.text: Copy the letter as it is into the new model
choices.why: That carries Coleta's words past the border, which is exactly the leak the layer exists to stop.

choices.text: Ask Coleta to resend the row in a known format
choices.why: CDC runs one way, outwards; Coleta is not asked to change anything.

choices.text: Put the record in a queue for a person, and say so
choices.why: Right: the layer refuses what it does not understand. A person finds out what the letter means, and that becomes a new test.

prompt: In phase 2 someone proposes that the new correction screen also call a Coleta program directly, so Coleta has each correction at once. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Nothing, since Coleta would be minutes closer to the truth
choices.why: Being minutes closer is bought with the chance of never arriving at all, silently.

choices.text: When the second write fails, the two disagree and nothing records it
choices.why: Right: two systems that share no transaction. Write once, to the master, and let the copy follow from its record of changes.

choices.text: Coleta's programs cannot be called from outside the IBM i
choices.why: The bus already calls Coleta for farm lookup. The objection is not reach but the second write.

choices.text: The clerks would see two confirmations
choices.why: They would see one, a saved correction, which is the trouble when Coleta never got it.

prompt: In the shadow calculation's first month, 17 farms differed from Coleta by six centavos or less, all from rounding. Why did Marcos not set a tolerance of ten centavos?

choices.text: Because the law forbids any difference in a farm's payment
choices.why: No law is cited. The objection is about what a tolerance would hide.

choices.text: Because ten centavos was too large, and two would have done
choices.why: The size of the tolerance is not the point; any tolerance passes the 17 without anybody deciding.

choices.text: Because the 17 were a defect on the new side
choices.why: They were a difference of method, and neither side was wrong; that is why it needed a decision.

choices.text: Because a tolerance hides what needs deciding
choices.why: Right: it would hide that the two worked differently, and somebody had to decide which was right. He decided the replacement rounds per collection, like Coleta, since farmers compare statements and a change of method is announced.

prompt: Put the steps of switching Coleta off in the order lesson 13 plans them.
items: Stop the inputs: nothing new is forwarded or written
Make it read-only, with history still visible
Archive what must be kept, under the retention rules
Power the IBM i down, kept intact for a period
End the contracts, licences, flows and accounts around it
trap: Each step stays reversible until the machine is off, and the contracts end last; that fifth step is the one migrations forget, and where the money is.

prompt: Joana's monthly report counts capabilities the new systems serve, but puts first the measure that cannot be reached while Coleta is still needed: what has been ___.

1,958 farms are in scope and 7 duplicates are merged into their survivors. Suppose 3 farms had been rejected with a reason on the night. How many farms should the reconciliation then expect to find in the target?
A faulty load divides every farm's litres by 100 once too often. The number of rows is right. Which is the first of the three reconciliation levels to catch it?

choices.text: The count
choices.why: Every row arrived, so the counts agree. A count cannot see a row with the wrong value in it.

choices.text: None, since each row is well formed
choices.why: Well formed is not the same as right. The litres no longer add up to what the source sent.

choices.text: The control total of the litres
choices.why: Right: a unit divided once too often moves the sum. The record level would catch it too, but the total sees it first.

choices.text: Only the record-by-record fingerprints
choices.why: Fingerprints are needed for errors that cancel out, like litres moved between farms. This one does not cancel.

prompt: The mapping puts the fat result into the protein field, and the reconciliation's rules were written from the same specification. All three levels pass. What catches it?

choices.text: Running the reconciliation again with a different hash
choices.why: A different hash compares the same wrong rule on both sides. The reconciliation agrees with the specification, mistakes included.

choices.text: A larger count, over every collection row
choices.why: Counts see missing and extra rows. Nothing is missing here.

choices.text: The load's own error log
choices.why: The load did exactly what it was told. A wrong rule produces no error.

choices.text: Cláudia's team reading 40 random farms beside Coleta
choices.why: Right: an owner who knows milk sees that a farm's fat does not look like its fat. A wrong rule shows in every farm it touches, so a small sample finds it.

prompt: Nine farms have CPFs with wrong check digits. A developer proposes fixing them in the transformation, so the new system receives them correct. Why did Serra Alta fix them in Coleta instead?

choices.text: Because Coleta still writes them into every file
choices.why: Right: Coleta keeps running for months, and a fact fixed only in flight stays wrong there. Under the strangler it still writes SAP's nightly file. A wrong fact is corrected where it lives, by its owner; a wrong form is translated in flight.

choices.text: Because the transformation cannot check digits
choices.why: The mapping already refuses a CPF whose check digits fail. Checking is easy; the question is where the fix lives.

choices.text: Because cleansing after the load is cheaper
choices.why: After the load the new system starts dirty in front of its users. And Coleta would still be wrong.

choices.text: Because finance does not sign rules in the specification
choices.why: Finance signs the tax ids. The reason is the source's life, not who signs.

prompt: To keep the night moving, someone suggests a default row in the municipality table: any spelling it does not know becomes Juiz de Fora. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Juiz de Fora is not in the IBGE table
choices.why: It is; the problem is not the value but that one is invented at all.

choices.text: Tomorrow's new misspelling becomes a farm in the wrong town, silently
choices.why: Right: refusal is what makes the table safe. A default is a value somebody will later believe.

choices.text: A default row slows the load down
choices.why: The cost is not speed. It loads quickly and wrongly.

choices.text: The 97 spellings would all map to it
choices.why: The 97 known spellings have their own rows. Only unknown ones fall to the default.

prompt: After the go decision, at which moment does rolling back to Coleta stop being a rollback and become a fix forward?

choices.text: At 10:00 on Sunday, when the window closes
choices.why: After the window, going back means carrying the new readings into Coleta. It is costly and still possible.

choices.text: At the go decision itself, at 05:00
choices.why: The go makes rollback dearer, not impossible; a procedure for carrying readings back was rehearsed.

choices.text: When the first bank file from the new system goes out on the 9th
choices.why: Right: undoing it would mean asking about 1,900 farms to return money. So the last decision to go back is on the 8th.

choices.text: When hypercare ends after eight weeks
choices.why: By then two payments have gone. The point of no return came with the first.

prompt: Put these steps of Serra Alta's cutover night in the order of the runbook.
items: Freeze Coleta; the handhelds hold their readings
Take the final extract and load it
Reconcile at all three levels
Switch the integrations to the new system
Decide go or no-go against the written criteria
trap: Nothing is loaded before the freeze, nothing is decided before the proof, and the integrations are switched before the decision so the smoke test can run.

prompt: The binder suggests a farm's tax id is unique, and a developer adds a unique constraint on it in the new system. What would the 38 shared tax ids have done on the night?

choices.text: Nothing: they are all the same tank registered twice
choices.why: Only 7 are. The other 31 are one producer with two properties, two tanks and two payments.

choices.text: Merged the 31 producers' two farms and paid each once
choices.why: A constraint refuses; it does not merge. The silent merge was the danger of a merge rule, not of this.

choices.text: Loaded cleanly, since the profile had already fixed them
choices.why: A profile measures; it fixes nothing. The 31 are correct as two farms and stay that way.

choices.text: Failed the load for 31 legitimate producers' second farms
choices.why: Right: the duplicate is a rule the binder implied and the world does not keep. Only the person who registered them knew which shared ids were real.

prompt: Option A's subscription costs R$ 25 × 1,900 farms a month from signature, and the first farm payment is in month 10. If implementation slipped by two months, moving the first payment to month 12, how many reais of subscription would be paid before the product paid a farm?
By the copy test, which of these is core for Serra Alta?

choices.text: Issuing an NF-e for every sale
choices.why: Mission-critical, and context: a dairy that cannot invoice cannot ship, and invoicing well wins no shelf.

choices.text: The calculation that applies the tables to litres and lab results
choices.why: Every dairy does it the same way and several products already do it. A competitor who bought one would have it.

choices.text: Paying 3,200 employees on time
choices.why: Payroll is the lesson's example of mission-critical context, the natural home of a bought product.

choices.text: The bonus tables, with thirty years of each farm's lab history
choices.why: Right: a competitor who bought any software at all would still not have them. The differentiator is the policy, and a policy is data.

prompt: Joana's first numbers were the vendor's R$ 2,070,000 and her own build estimate. Which of these did the vendor's proposal leave out? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The interfaces to SAP, the lab and Rota
choices.why: Right: a product arrives with an API, not with interfaces to your systems, R$ 240,000 on A's sheet.

choices.text: Maintenance at 20% of the build a year
choices.why: That is the builder's blind spot, on C's sheet. A product's vendor maintains the product.

choices.text: The bill growing as 100 farms a year are added
choices.why: Right: the metric is per active farm, and the proposal priced 1,900 farms for three years.

choices.text: Somebody on call during payment week
choices.why: On-call is what builders forget; on A the vendor runs the product, and Serra Alta watches its interfaces.

prompt: A director says Serra Alta has no plan to leave, so A's exit should count at 20% of R$ 397,800. Why does the sheet keep it whole?

choices.text: Because the law requires the full exit to be booked
choices.why: No law is cited; the argument is about what a guess hides and what a door costs.

choices.text: Because the door's price matters even if unused
choices.why: Right: a guessed probability hides inside a precise-looking number, and a dearer door gives the vendor power at every renewal. The exit is what the option costs to stay out of a corner, whether or not anybody walks through the door.

choices.text: Because leaving is certain at the end of the term
choices.why: Nobody claims it is certain. The point is that the price matters even if it is never paid.

choices.text: Because B and C have no exit, so only A carries one
choices.why: All three carry one: B R$ 190,000 and C R$ 307,000.

prompt: Option A's first term is 24 months, with six months' notice to leave at its end. Why does the record put a date of 31 May in somebody's calendar?

choices.text: Because the vendor deletes the data 90 days after that date
choices.why: The 90 days run from the end of the contract, not from 31 May.

choices.text: Because the price cap expires on that day
choices.why: The 4% cap applies at the renewal; 31 May is about the notice.

choices.text: Because that is when S/4HANA goes live
choices.why: S/4HANA is planned for January 2028 and concerns option B.

choices.text: Because notice is due by the end of month 18
choices.why: Right: the cheapest moment to reconsider is just before notice is due. The notice period is the part of lock-in that shows as a date, and missing the end of month 18 commits R$ 655,200.

prompt: A loses to C only at R$ 40.14 per farm per month, yet the record's trigger to revisit is a renewal offer above R$ 32. Why set it lower?

choices.text: Because R$ 32 is the price the vendor quoted for year 3
choices.why: Year 3 is R$ 26 with the 4% cap. R$ 32 is Serra Alta's own line.

choices.text: Because the exit is decided six months before renewal
choices.why: Right: an alternative has to be prepared before the price forces it, and a trigger at break-even would fire when it is already too late to act on it.

choices.text: Because a 61% rise is impossible under the contract
choices.why: The cap covers the first renewal. The trigger is about having time, not about what is possible.

choices.text: Because the sheet's figures are too rough to trust near 40
choices.why: The arithmetic is checked cell by cell. The margin is for time, not for doubt about the sums.

prompt: On A's exit, why is only 60% of the R$ 240,000 integration line rebuilt?

choices.text: Because the vendor rebuilds the other 40% as part of the export
choices.why: The vendor sells the export of the history, R$ 30,000. Interfaces are Serra Alta's.

choices.text: Because 40% of the interfaces are no longer needed after three years
choices.why: SAP, the lab and Rota are all still there. What changes is which side of the layer is rewritten.

choices.text: Because interfaces talk to Serra Alta's model, not to the product
choices.why: Right: an anti-corruption layer stands between them, and only its product-facing side is rewritten. R$ 96,000 of lock-in removed by design, and the same thing lets Serra Alta negotiate a renewal as somebody who could leave.

choices.text: Because the integration line includes a one-off licence
choices.why: It is work on interfaces, R$ 30,000 a month for eight months. No licence in it.

prompt: A board member compares the three options' spending at month 6 and proposes B, the lowest at that point. What does lesson 15's curve over time say?

choices.text: B stays cheapest, since its licences are smaller
choices.why: B passes C in month 13, as custom development runs at full speed, and ends the highest of the three.

choices.text: B is cheapest only early; by month 36 it is the dearest
choices.why: Right: early spending on consultants and licences hides what the custom work costs later. The shape decides whether a ranking means anything.

choices.text: The month does not matter, since totals are what rank options
choices.why: Totals rank; the shape over time, the dates and the sensitivity decide whether the ranking means anything. Month 6 is a misleading slice.

choices.text: C is cheapest at month 6, so the comparison was mistaken
choices.why: At month 6 C has spent the most, R$ 1,233,000. B was lowest then, and that is the trap.
